title: Hardwired against Microprogrammed: Speed, Cost and Flexibility
quickIdea: Hardwired control is the fastest and the least flexible; horizontal microcode is next fastest and still flexible; vertical microcode is slowest because of its decoders. The choice follows the instruction set: small and fixed goes hardwired, large and changeable goes microprogrammed.
remember: Speed order, and it is asked directly: hardwired, then horizontal microprogrammed, then vertical microprogrammed.
Hardwired wins on speed and chip area, loses on flexibility: a new instruction means new wiring.
Microprogrammed wins on flexibility and on handling complex instruction sets, loses on speed and on chip area for the control store.
The association to keep: RISC designs tend to be hardwired, CISC designs microprogrammed - but the association is a tendency, not a rule.
A writable control store lets a machine emulate another instruction set by loading a different microprogram, which is the one thing hardwired control cannot do.

example.prompt: A designer must add a new string-compare instruction to an existing processor. Which control unit makes this cheap, and what does the other one cost?
example.work: With a microprogrammed unit the new instruction is a new microroutine in the control store, plus one entry in the mapping; no wiring changes. With a hardwired unit every control signal the new instruction uses must gain another AND term, and the state machine may need new states.
example.answer: Microprogrammed control makes it a software change; hardwired control makes it a re-design of the signal trees and possibly of the state machine.

gateAngle: GATE CSE 1987 Q.1(vi) asks which statement about a microprogrammed control unit is true, and only 'facilitates easy implementation of new instructions' is. GATE CSE 1999 Q.2.19 asks for the speed order and the answer is hardwired, horizontal, vertical. Both questions are decided by the two facts on this card, not by any arithmetic.

variations.label: VERIFIED PYQ
variations.question: GATE CSE 1987 Q.1(vi): a microprogrammed control unit (1) is faster than a hard-wired control unit (2) facilitates easy implementation of new instructions (3) is useful when very small programs are to be run (4) usually refers to the control unit of a microprocessor.
variations.why: Microcode is slower than hardwired logic, and small programs are exactly where the control store's cost is not justified. A microprocessor's control unit may be built either way, so statement 4 is false too.

variations.label: VERIFIED PYQ
variations.question: GATE CSE 1999 Q.2.19: arrange hardwired control, vertical microprogramming and horizontal microprogramming in decreasing order of operating speed.
variations.answer: Hardwired control, horizontal microprogramming, vertical microprogramming.
variations.why: Hardwired has no control-store access at all; horizontal has the access but no decoder in the signal path; vertical adds the decoder delay on top of the access.

variations.label: PREDICTED VARIATION
variations.question: A machine must run programs compiled for an older instruction set. Which control unit makes that possible without a second processor, and why?
variations.answer: A microprogrammed unit with a writable control store: load the old instruction set's microprogram and the same hardware executes the old instructions.
variations.why: Emulation is a property of storing the control as data. Hardwired control would need the old instruction set built into the silicon as well.

trap.what: Saying a microprogrammed unit is faster because it is 'programmed' and programs are efficient.
trap.why: The program is not an optimisation: it adds a memory read and, for vertical microcode, a decode to every control signal's path.
trap.counterexample: Two identical datapaths, one driven hardwired and one driven from a control store, run at different clock rates for the same logic depth - the microprogrammed one cannot be faster, because it does strictly more work per control word.

check.question: Give the speed order of the three control organisations and the one-sentence reason for each step in it.
check.answer: Hardwired, then horizontal microprogrammed, then vertical microprogrammed: no store access, then a store access with no decoder, then a store access plus a decoder.
check.explanation: Each step down the order adds one delay to the path from the state or the store to the datapath.
